t: #3604 Minimum Time to Reach Destination in Directed Graph
o: We start at node 0 at time 0 and want the earliest arrival at node n-1. Waiting is free, so from state (node, earliest arrival time d) an edge usable on [start, end] can be taken iff d <= end, and departing at max(d, start) arrives at max(d, start) + 1. This is exactly Dijkstra on arrival times: earliest arrivals dominate, so the first time we settle node n-1 is optimal. Edges and nodes are up to 1e5, so an O(E log E) Dijkstra fits.
k: Waiting makes the transition deterministic: departure time = max(arrival, start), requiring arrival <= end.
Earliest-arrival labels are monotone, so Dijkstra with the modified relaxation is correct.
No negative or zero-length complications: each traversal costs exactly 1.

a.i: Standard Dijkstra where relaxing edge (u, v, s, e) from label d checks d <= e and proposes nd = max(d, s) + 1. Since nd >= d + 1 > d, edge weights are positive and the greedy invariant holds.
s: Build adjacency lists of (to, start, end).
Run a min-heap Dijkstra from node 0 with dist[0] = 0.
Relax each outgoing edge only if d <= end; candidate = max(d, start) + 1.
a.t: O(E log E) — each edge relaxes at most once per improved label, heap operations dominate.
a.sp: O(N + E) for adjacency, distances, and heap.

w: The only twist on vanilla Dijkstra is the max(d, start) departure rule; correctness follows because arrival times only increase along a path. Pitfall: using strict d < end instead of d <= end, and forgetting that waiting before an early-start edge is allowed. Follow-up: what if travel times differ per edge (still Dijkstra with nd = max(d, s) + w, checking d + w <= e + slack semantics carefully).
